landing.title: Yawaragi
landing.intro: Explore Japanese sake through guided flavor profiles, label scans, and a chat that learns what you enjoy. Built for the curious — at any starting point.
landing.sectionScanBody: Point your camera at a bottle. We read the kanji and surface what's known about the brewery, the rice, and the style.
landing.sectionChatBody: Tell us what you usually drink. We translate it into Japanese brewer vocabulary and suggest sake that fits.
landing.sectionProfileBody: Over time, your reactions shape a personal flavor map you can compare with others.

landing.heading: Know what's in the cup.
landing.lead: Point your phone at a sake label. Yawaragi tells you what it is, how it tastes, and whether you'll like it. One tap and it's in your journal.
landing.sampleLink: Or look through a sample collection
landing.smallPrint: Free · no account needed · for adults 18+
landing.featureIdentifyBody: Kanji or romaji — the camera reads whichever the bottle gives you. No camera? Use a photo or type the name.

landing.privacyBody: Everything works on your phone without an account. Nothing is posted publicly, and your ratings are only shared — anonymously — if you choose to.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.intro: Yawaragi is operated by the maintainer named in the Impressum, who acts as the data controller under GDPR Art. 4(7). This page lists the categories of personal data we process and the third-party processors we rely on. It is updated alongside every release that introduces or changes a processing operation, per ADR-0009.
privacy.anonymousSessionBody: When you use a feature that calls a paid AI service (today: the label scan), we set a signed, opaque cookie named `yawaragi_session` with a 24-hour sliding lifetime. The cookie holds a random identifier — never your name, email, or IP. We use it together with a short-lived hash of your IP address (kept only as a query key, never stored as plaintext and never written to a database or log) to cap how many scans a single visitor can run per day, so the AI bill stays bounded. Lawful basis: legitimate interest in cost protection of paid AI surfaces (GDPR Art. 6(1)(f)). Retention: 24 hours, sliding. Data residency: EU (rate-limit storage hosted in an EU region of Upstash Redis).
privacy.processorVercel: Vercel, Inc. (USA) — hosting, build, and edge logs. Transfer mechanism: EU-US Data Privacy Framework plus EU SCCs as a fallback. Vercel processes service-generated data (request logs, build metadata) as an independent controller.
privacy.processorSupabase: Supabase, Inc. — Postgres database for the Sakenowa reference mirror and (from Phase 2.5) user-scoped tables. Project region: eu-central-1 (Frankfurt). Transfer mechanism: EU SCCs (Modules 2 and 3) governed by Irish law. Service usage telemetry is processed by Supabase as an independent controller under Art. 6(1)(f) (billing, security, service improvement). Breach notification SLA: 48 hours.
privacy.processorUpstash: Upstash, Inc. — Redis key-value store hosted in an EU region (e.g. eu-central-1 Frankfurt) used as the rate-limit budget store for the anonymous-session cookie described above. Stored data: the salted SHA-256 hash of the visitor IP and the opaque session id, each with a 24-hour TTL. No plaintext IPs, no account identifiers. Transfer mechanism: EU SCCs (data does not leave the EU region). Data Processing Agreement: pending signature before Production deployment.
privacy.processorClerk: Clerk, Inc. (USA) — user authentication (sign-in, session, JWT issuance) starting Phase 2.5. Data categories: email address, given name, family name, and short-lived email-verification codes used to confirm sign-in. Lawful basis: Art. 6(1)(b) (performance of contract — Clerk holds the credentials required to operate an account). Transfer mechanism: EU-US Data Privacy Framework plus EU SCCs as a fallback. Retention: until account deletion or 24 months of account inactivity (per ADR-0009). Clerk does not publish a fixed breach-notification SLA; per the breach runbook, we treat an unconfirmed Clerk incident as starting an internal 24-hour clock toward BayLDA Art. 33 notification.
privacy.sakenowaNote: Sake brand and brewery reference data is mirrored from the public Sakenowa Data API (muro.sakenowa.com). The mirror itself contains no personal data.
privacy.retention: Cookies expire after one year. Phase 2 reference data is retained for the lifetime of the service. Future per-user data (Phase 2.5+) follows the retention rules in ADR-0009.
privacy.contact: For data-subject requests (access, rectification, erasure, portability), use the email address in the Impressum.

temperatureTerms.title: Serving temperatures
temperatureTerms.intro: Sake is served across a range of temperatures, and each step has a Japanese name. The degrees are approximate; what matters is how the same sake changes from one step to the next.

notes.yukibie: Snow-chilled: as cold as it gets. Aroma is muted and the finish turns sharp and clean.
notes.hanabie: Flower-chilled: cold from the fridge. Crisp, with the aroma still held back.
notes.suzuhie: Cool, just under room temperature. The aroma starts to open while it stays fresh.
notes.joon: Room temperature: the sake as it is, with nothing hidden or added.
notes.nurukan: Lukewarm, a little above body heat. Rounder and softer; umami comes forward.
notes.atsukan: Hot. Drier and sharper, best with fuller, savory sakes.

learn.title: Learn
learn.metaDescription: What the words on a sake label mean: grades, polishing, yeast starters, unpasteurised, aged and sparkling sake, and sake rice. Written by hand, with sources.
learn.lead: What the words on a label mean. Written by hand, with sources.

how-to-read-a-label.title: How to read a label
how-to-read-a-label.answer: The biggest characters are usually the sake’s name, not the brewery. The grade, the polishing ratio and the details sit smaller, often on the back label.

name.note: The sake’s name. The brewery’s own name is printed small, next to its address.

type.note: One of the two is on every bottle.

grade.note: Alone or combined, as here. No grade word at all means ordinary sake, futsūshu 普通酒.

polishing.note: How much of each grain is left after milling. 60% means 40% was milled away.

ingredients.value: 米, 米こうじ, sometimes 醸造アルコール
ingredients.note: Rice, kōji rice, and brewer’s alcohol when it was added. Water is not listed.

alcohol.note: 度 is percent. Undiluted sake, genshu, runs higher.

volume.note: The two common bottles: 四合瓶 yongōbin and 一升瓶 isshōbin.

date.note: When it was bottled for sale, not when it was brewed. Printing it became optional with the 2022 revision of the labelling standard.

maker.note: 酒造 shuzō and 醸造 jōzō both mean brewery.

styles.note: Short words, often in a corner or on a neck label. Each has its own page here.

detail.p1: A front label is made to be recognised, not read: a name in brush calligraphy, sometimes nothing else. The facts are on the back label or on a narrow strip at the side.
detail.p2: If you can find only three things, find the grade, the polishing ratio and the character 生. Together they tell you roughly how the sake was made and whether it belongs in the fridge.

grades.title: Grades at a glance
grades.answer: Eight grade names, built from two questions: was brewer’s alcohol added, and how far was the rice polished? Sake that carries none of them is futsūshu, ordinary sake.

tokubetsuJunmai.value: 60% or less, or a special method
tokubetsuJunmai.note: The label has to say what makes it special.

honjozo.note: With a little brewer’s alcohol, like the three below.

tokubetsuHonjozo.value: 60% or less, or a special method

detail.p1: The percentages are polishing ratios: the share of each grain that remains after milling.
detail.p2: All eight share three rules. The rice must be inspected and graded 3 or better. Kōji rice must make up at least 15% of the rice. Any added alcohol may not exceed 10% of the rice’s weight.
detail.p3: A grade is a recipe, not a ranking. A lower number is not a better sake, only a different one.

junmai.title: Junmai
junmai.answer: Made only from rice, kōji and water, with no added brewer’s alcohol.

polishing.note: The ratio is still printed on the label.

detail.p1: The word joins the other grades. Junmai ginjō and junmai daiginjō are ginjō and daiginjō made without added alcohol.
detail.p2: With nothing added, junmai sake tends to show the flavor of the rice and the kōji more than other kinds do.

ginjo.title: Ginjō and daiginjō
ginjo.answer: Rice polished to 60% or less and brewed with the ginjō method. Daiginjō takes the polishing to 50% or less.

method.note: A slow fermentation at low temperature.

alcohol.value: Allowed, up to 10% of the rice’s weight
alcohol.note: Without it: junmai ginjō, junmai daiginjō.

aroma.note: The fruity aroma the method is known for.

detail.p1: Polishing removes the outer layers of the grain, which hold most of its protein. Too much protein gives rough, unrefined flavors; what is left after polishing is mostly starch.
detail.p2: A lower number is not a better sake, only a different one.

honjozo.title: Honjōzō
honjozo.answer: Rice polished to 70% or less, with a small, limited amount of brewer’s alcohol added.

alcohol.value: Up to 10% of the rice’s weight
alcohol.note: Brewer’s alcohol: distilled alcohol, added to the mash before pressing.

tokubetsu.value: 60% or less, or a special method
tokubetsu.note: The label has to say which.

detail.p1: Added to the mash, the alcohol draws out aroma. It also thins what comes from the rice and the fermentation, so the sake has less acidity and umami and feels lighter.
detail.p2: It is an ingredient with a limit, not a shortcut. Above the limit a sake cannot carry any of the eight grade names.

polishing-ratio.title: Polishing ratio
polishing-ratio.answer: The percentage of each rice grain that is left after milling. 60% means 40% was milled away.

junmai.note: Whatever the ratio is, the label states it.

detail.p1: The outer layers of a grain hold protein, and too much protein gives rough, unrefined flavors, called zatsumi 雑味. Milling them away leaves the starchy centre.
detail.p2: The number describes the rice, not the result. Sake experts treat it as a pointer to a sake’s character, not as a measure of its quality.

yeast-starters.title: Starters: sokujō, kimoto, yamahai
yeast-starters.answer: Before the main mash, brewers grow yeast in a small starter. It needs lactic acid to keep other microbes out, and the three methods differ in where that acid comes from.

sokujo.note: About two weeks. The method most sake uses today.

kimoto.note: About four weeks. The rice and kōji are first ground to a paste with poles.

yamahai.value: Wild lactic bacteria, without the grinding
yamahai.note: About four weeks. Worked out in 1909 as a simpler kimoto.

detail.p1: In kimoto and yamahai the starter begins cold, at about 8°C, and is warmed slowly. Lactic bacteria come first and sour the mash. The yeast is added about two weeks in, and the acid and the alcohol then kill the bacteria off.
detail.p2: Sokujō adds ready-made lactic acid instead of growing the bacteria, which takes about two weeks off the starter.
detail.p3: The slower methods tend to give a fuller body and a more complex flavor; sokujō tends to be lighter and more delicate. The starter is separate from the grade: a junmai ginjō can be a kimoto.

nama.title: Nama: unpasteurised sake
nama.answer: Sake is normally pasteurised twice, before storage and at bottling. Nama sake skips one or both, which keeps it fresh-tasting and means it has to stay cold.

namazake.note: Never pasteurised. Its label has to carry a storage warning.

namachozo.note: Stored unpasteurised, then pasteurised once at bottling.

namazume.note: Pasteurised once before storage, then bottled without a second heating.

hiyaoroshi.note: A nama-zume aged from winter and released in autumn.

detail.p1: Pasteurising heats sake to about 60–65°C. It kills microbes and stops the enzymes that would otherwise keep changing the sake in the bottle.
detail.p2: With its enzymes still active, namazake tastes fresh and lively, and keeps only in the fridge.

muroka.title: Muroka
muroka.answer: “Unfiltered”: sake that skips the second filtration, the one with charcoal. It is still pressed and clear, not cloudy.

skipped.note: Charcoal takes out color and adjusts flavor.

kept.note: A cloth still separates the sake from the lees, so some filtering does happen.

combined.note: Three style words in one: muroka, nama, genshu.

detail.p1: The word has no single fixed meaning. For one brewer it means no secondary filtration at all, for another only no charcoal.
detail.p2: Muroka sake is considered fuller in flavor: it keeps the fine particles, aromas and flavors that charcoal would take out.

genshu.title: Genshu
genshu.answer: Undiluted sake: no water is added after pressing to bring the alcohol down.

rule.note: A sake may still be called genshu if added water changes its alcohol by less than one point.

detail.p1: Sake comes off the press at around 17–20% alcohol. Without the water, genshu keeps that strength and a stronger taste.

nigori.title: Nigori
nigori.answer: Cloudy sake: the mash is pressed through a coarse mesh, so rice solids and yeast pass into the bottle.

mesh.value: Depends on how coarse the mesh is

pasteurised.note: It used to be sold unpasteurised, with living yeast.

live.note: An unpasteurised nigori whose yeast keeps working in the bottle, so it is fizzy.

detail.p1: Nigori and muroka are different things. Muroka is about the charcoal filtration after pressing; nigori is about the mesh at the press.

koshu.title: Koshu: aged sake
koshu.answer: Sake matured for years rather than months. It turns from yellow to amber and takes on aromas of caramel, dried fruit, nuts and soy sauce.

usual.value: Six months to a year before release

koshu.note: No law fixes a number. The makers’ association writes “more than two years” in its glossary and “at least three” in its guide.

printedAge.note: Fractions are dropped, and a blend states the age of its youngest part.

detail.p1: The color and the flavor come from a slow reaction between the sugars and the amino acids in the sake, the same one that browns bread.
detail.p2: Koshu has a slightly bitter taste and a long finish. Bitterness is not usually wanted in sake; here it is part of the style.

sparkling.title: Sparkling sake
sparkling.answer: Sake with bubbles. The kinds differ in where the gas comes from: injected, made by a second fermentation, or still being made by live yeast in the bottle.

carbonated.note: Added under pressure once the sake is made and filtered. Usually clear, and usually pasteurised.

secondFermentation.value: Fermented again in the bottle or a sealed tank
secondFermentation.note: Fermentation is stopped early and finished under seal, which traps the gas. The sediment can stay, for a cloudy style, or be removed.

live.note: Bottled after only a coarse filtering and unpasteurised, so kōji and yeast keep working. A winter seasonal.

awa.note: Bubbles from fermentation only, clear, pasteurised, more than 10% alcohol, and 3.5 bar of pressure at 20°C. Set by the Japan Awasake Association, founded in 2016.

detail.p1: Strength varies widely. Many sparkling sakes are between 5% and 12%, lighter than still sake; the sweet ones sit around 6–8%, and there are strong, dry ones too.
detail.p2: How sparkling sake is made is not tightly regulated, and there are no standard label terms for it. The back label and the maker’s own notes are the guide.

sake-rice.title: Sake rice
sake-rice.answer: Brewers prefer rice bred for the job: large grains with a white, starchy core and little protein. A few varieties appear on labels again and again.

yamadaNishiki.note: The most widely grown sake rice. Crossed in 1923, recommended by the prefecture since 1936.

miyamaNishiki.note: Named in 1978. Hardy in the cold, and grown across Nagano and the north-east.

omachi.note: Found in 1859 and an ancestor of the first two. Nearly all of it is still grown in Okayama.

detail.p1: The white core is called shinpaku 心白: a loose, opaque pocket of starch at the centre of the grain, which kōji mould grows into easily. “Large” has a definition too: 26 grams or more per thousand grains.
detail.p2: A variety may be named on a label only when it makes up more than half of the rice used, and the label must then give its share.
detail.p3: Varieties differ in how readily they dissolve in the mash, and that shows in the sake. Each region has its own.

serving-temperatures.title: Serving temperatures
serving-temperatures.answer: Sake is served anywhere from about 5°C to 55°C, and each step has a Japanese name. The degrees are typical, not exact.

yukihie.note: Much colder and it is hard to taste sake at all.

joon.note: Kept out of the fridge and served as it is.

jokan.note: Warmed sake is normally heated to about 42–45°C.

detail.p1: Chilling suits fragrant and fresh sake. Ginjō and unpasteurised sake are usually served slightly chilled, at around 8–10°C, because their fruitiness and freshness are lost when warm.
detail.p2: Warming, kan 燗, is the traditional way to drink sake. Sweetness is sensed more strongly near body temperature while acidity hardly changes, so a sake that is low in sweetness and a little high in acidity, as junmai often is, comes into balance when warmed.
detail.p3: Heated too far, the alcohol turns strong and covers the sake’s delicate aromas.

flavor-words.title: The six flavor words
flavor-words.answer: Six Japanese brewers’ terms that Sakenowa uses to chart a sake’s flavor. The English words on Yawaragi’s charts are approximations of them, not translations.

f1.note: Fruit and blossom on the nose. Not perfumed.

f5.note: The closest of the six to a Western word.

f6.note: A refreshing finish, with little left behind.

detail.p1: Sakenowa is a Japanese sake community. It works the six values out by analysing what its users write about each sake, so a chart shows how people describe a sake. It is not a laboratory measurement.
detail.p2: The six do not line up with wine vocabulary. Read each English word as pointing at the right idea, not as matching it.
detail.p3: On Yawaragi the picture built from these six is the flavor chart (Sakenowa). The method and the data behind it are Sakenowa’s.

other-japanese-drinks.title: Sake and the other Japanese drinks
other-japanese-drinks.answer: Sake is brewed from rice, rice koji and water. Shochu and awamori are distilled. Umeshu is ume fruit steeped in a liquor and sweetened, which makes it a liqueur.

sake.note: Rice, rice koji and water, fermented and strained; under 22% alcohol.

craftSake.note: Brewed from rice with a step the legal definition of sake does not allow, such as fruit or herbs in the ferment, so its label does not say 清酒.

shochu.note: Pot-distilled shochu is up to 45% alcohol; shochu from a continuous still is under 36%.

awamori.note: A pot-distilled shochu made in Okinawa from rice koji grown with black koji and water.

umeshu.note: Ume fruit steeped in a liquor, with sugar added; its label says リキュール.

liqueur.note: Made from a liquor and sugar or other ingredients, with at least 2% extract.

detail.p1: Japanese law sorts every drink into a category, and the bottle must print it in Japanese on the side with the brand: 清酒 for sake, 焼酎 for shochu, リキュール for a liqueur. That word settles what is in the bottle, whoever made it.
detail.p2: Yawaragi's catalogue holds sake. A scan reads craft sake as sake; shochu, awamori, umeshu and other liqueurs have no page here.

notes.hanaabi: Pineapple and white grape, a soft sweetness, a short clean finish.
notes.jikonOmachi: Rounder than the Yamada Nishiki one: rice, melon, a little acidity at the end.
notes.shirakawago: Thick and sweet, a nigori. Not for me, at least not cold.
notes.aramasa: Sharp acidity, almost like a white wine. With food next time.

caveat.grade: {grade} is usually fragrant: pairings often given for {kind}.
caveat.chart: From the flavor chart (Sakenowa), for the whole line: pairings for {kind}. Bottlings vary.

sheet.title: Where these pairings come from
sheet.intro: These are general pairings for a kind of sake, not notes written for this one. Each kind comes from a named source: the Sake Service Institute’s types — kunshu (薫酒) fragrant, soshu (爽酒) light, junshu (醇酒) rich — and published guidance for koshu, kijoshu, sparkling and nigori.

how.style: This bottling is {kind}. The foods are the ones the sources below give for it.
how.grade: This bottling is a {grade}. Ginjo grades are usually fragrant sake, {kind}, so the foods are the ones the sources below give for that kind. A restrained, dry ginjo may suit lighter dishes better.
how.chart: We compare this sake's flavor chart with the average of every sake in the catalogue and look for the one direction it clearly stands out in. That points to {kind}, and the foods are the ones the sources below give for that kind. The chart describes the whole line, so a bottling of it may differ.

sheet.startingPoint: They are starting points to try, not rules. Where the chart or the label says too little, we show none.

sashimi.name: Sashimi and other raw fish
sashimi.reason: Sake keeps raw fish from tasting fishy, and a delicate dish leaves its aroma room.

crab.name: Crab and sweet shellfish
crab.reason: Their gentle sweetness sits alongside the fruit without covering it.

freshCheese.name: Fresh, mild cheese, with tomato
freshCheese.reason: Mild and milky: nothing to drown the aroma.

oden.name: Oden and other dishes in dashi
oden.reason: Kelp and bonito broth: two umami sources that strengthen each other, met by an umami-rich sake.

sukiyaki.name: Sukiyaki
sukiyaki.reason: Soy sauce, like sake, is made with koji and yeast; their savory notes carry each other.

porkDaikon.name: Pork and daikon simmered in soy
porkDaikon.reason: Slow-cooked and savory, with the weight to stand beside a full sake.

coldTofu.name: Chilled tofu, hiyayakko
coldTofu.reason: Plain and cool, it lets a clean sake show.

oysters.name: Raw oysters
oysters.reason: Sake leaves less of the fishy note wine can bring out in shellfish.

friedFish.name: Fried white fish
friedFish.reason: A clean, dry finish cuts through the oil of the batter.

hardCheese.name: Hard, mature cheese: Comté, Parmesan, aged Cheddar
hardCheese.reason: Both come from long fermentation and aging; their savory, nutty notes meet.

unagi.name: Grilled eel, unagi
unagi.reason: A sweet soy glaze to match the sake's caramel depth.

driedFruit.name: Dried fruit and nuts
driedFruit.reason: They echo the dried-fruit notes that aging brings.

kijoshu.kind: kijoshu (貴醸酒), brewed with sake in place of some water

darkChocolate.name: Dark chocolate
darkChocolate.reason: Sweet and dense, it needs something as rich.

iceCream.name: Vanilla ice cream
iceCream.reason: Served beside it, or poured over it.

foieGras.name: Foie gras
foieGras.reason: Rich and fatty, the way sweet wine is served with it.

freshCheese.name: Fresh cheese: chèvre, ricotta
freshCheese.reason: Bubbles and a little sweetness lift a clean, milky cheese.

fruitDesserts.name: Fruit desserts
fruitDesserts.reason: A slightly sweet sparkling sake meets fruit.

sparkling.note: Often served as an aperitif, before the meal.

spicyDishes.name: Spicy dishes: curry, kimchi
spicyDishes.reason: Its sweetness and rice solids soften chili heat — less so in a strong, dry nigori.

washedRindCheese.name: Washed-rind cheese: Taleggio, Époisses
washedRindCheese.reason: A creamy body and a hint of sweetness soften a pungent cheese.

nigori.note: Nigori runs from sweet and creamy to dry; these suit the sweeter, creamier ones.
